https://www.ynetnews.com/article/rykymce.text: They came running, swimming and even floating on inner tubes. Within a short time, tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco into Ceuta, Spain’s enclave on the North African coast, entering by sea and through a breach in the border fence. Spanish security forces were overwhelmed, reception centers filled up and what began as a local emergency quickly became a crisis with repercussions across Europe. Ceuta, along with the Spanish enclave of Melilla, forms one of the world’s most unusual borders: European territory located on the African continent and surrounded by Morocco. For anyone who manages to cross into the enclave, the move means entering Spanish territory and, in effect, the European Union. For Madrid and Brussels, however, the tall fences, cameras and patrols are only the final layer of defense. The more important barrier lies on the other side, in the hands of Moroccan security forces. The reason for the latest surge remains unclear. Initially, it was attributed largely to rumors circulating on social media, smuggling networks and a misreading of a Spanish court ruling that restricted authorities’ ability to immediately return migrants who reached the enclaves by sea. But in the days that followed, suspicions grew that Rabat’s conduct had also played a decisive role. According to reports in the Spanish media, intelligence services concluded that Morocco had not organized the mass crossing in advance but had allowed it to happen. Moroccan border controls, according to that assessment, had been gradually relaxed during July and did little to stop the crowds on the day of the breach. Ceuta regional president Juan Jesús Vivas told the European Parliament this week that around 100 people were killed during the border rush and that between 3,000 and 5,000 migrants remained in the enclave. EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner called for trade and visa policy to be used to pressure Morocco, while Vivas declared: “Morocco is not a reliable country.” But the crisis raises a much broader question: How were so many people able to reach one of the region’s most heavily guarded borders at roughly the same time, and what happens to Europe when the country it relies on is unable, or unwilling, to stop them? The border that begins in Rabat Since the 2015 refugee crisis, Europe has increasingly sought to move its effective borders south and east. Instead of waiting for migrant boats to reach the shores of Italy, Spain or Greece, the European Union has invested heavily in countries of origin and transit. That money has gone toward training security forces, buying equipment, improving surveillance systems, combating smugglers, returning migrants to their home countries and preventing boats from leaving in the first place. Morocco is one of the central partners in this strategy. According to European Commission figures, between 2015 and 2021 the EU committed 234 million euros to migration-related projects in the kingdom. The money funded border management, efforts against smuggling and human trafficking, migrant protection, voluntary return programs and improvements to Morocco’s migration policy. In 2023, the EU launched another program worth 152 million euros aimed at strengthening Morocco’s ability to manage its borders, dismantle smuggling networks and return migrants to their countries of origin. That program formed part of a much larger cooperation package with Rabat worth 624 million euros. From Europe’s perspective, the logic is straightforward. It is cheaper to stop a boat before it leaves shore, or a group before it reaches the fence, than to deal with thousands of people who have already entered European territory, allow them to apply for asylum and then manage months or years of deportation proceedings and appeals. Morocco benefits as well, not only through money and equipment but also through its status as a strategic partner, access to European decision-makers and greater leverage in negotiations over trade, visas, investment and diplomatic issues. But that is also where the weakness lies. Once Europe entrusts part of its border control to another country, that country can decide how tightly to enforce the rules, and when to loosen them. The clearest precedent came in Ceuta in May 2021. Within about two days, roughly 8,000 people entered the enclave, including around 1,500 minors, after Moroccan security forces displayed what Spain described as unusual passivity. Many migrants simply walked along the shore or swam around the maritime barrier. The episode took place at the height of a diplomatic crisis. Spain had allowed Brahim Ghali, leader of the Polisario Front, which seeks independence for Western Sahara, to receive medical treatment secretly on Spanish territory. Morocco, which considers Western Sahara an integral part of its territory, reacted furiously. Spanish Defense Minister Margarita Robles accused Rabat at the time of “blackmail,” saying it was using migrants and minors to pressure Spain. The European Parliament later condemned what it described as Morocco’s use of border control and migration, particularly unaccompanied minors, as a tool of political pressure against an EU member state. Morocco rejected the accusations. But the message was unmistakable in Madrid: Spain’s borders depended not only on the number of police officers, soldiers and fences on the Spanish side, but also on the state of relations with Rabat. The following year, Spain changed its long-standing position on Western Sahara and backed Morocco’s autonomy plan as a basis for resolving the conflict. Relations improved, and border cooperation strengthened. That does not mean every migration surge from Morocco is orchestrated by the government. Rabat itself faces pressure from young Moroccans who want to leave, smuggling networks and thousands of migrants arriving from sub-Saharan Africa. But the events of 2021 demonstrated how even a temporary and unofficial reduction in enforcement can become a European crisis within hours. From Tunisia to Mauritania Morocco is far from the only country involved in this model. In recent years, the European Union has signed a series of agreements with North African and Sahel countries combining economic aid and investment with commitments to curb irregular migration. In 2023, Europe signed a memorandum of understanding with Tunisia that included 105 million euros in migration support, almost three times the country’s average annual funding in that field during the previous two years. The money was intended to strengthen borders, combat smugglers, return migrants and prevent deaths at sea. Mauritania, which has become a major departure point for boats heading toward the Canary Islands, entered a migration partnership with the EU in 2024 backed by a 210 million euro assistance package. Not all of that money was earmarked for migration. It also covered humanitarian aid, jobs and security. But a major part of the program focused on border control, disrupting smuggling networks and stopping boats from heading into the Atlantic. Egypt was also elevated to strategic-partner status. An EU support package for Cairo announced in 2024 totaled 7.4 billion euros in loans, investments and grants. Around 200 million euros in grants were designated for migration management. For Europe, Egypt’s economic stability, in a country of more than 100 million people that has also received refugees and asylum seekers from across the region, became an internal security concern. Brussels presents such deals as broad partnerships covering infrastructure, energy, education and employment, not simply payments to block migrants. They are also based on the argument that migration cannot be addressed without tackling its underlying drivers, including poverty, war, unemployment and instability. In practice, however, one of the key measures by which these arrangements are judged is whether they reduce the number of boats reaching European shores. Erdoğan’s ‘open gates’ and Lukashenko’s ‘hybrid attack’ Turkey demonstrated more explicitly than almost any other country how migration can be turned into leverage in relations with Europe. Under a 2016 agreement, Ankara agreed to take back migrants who reached Greece irregularly, while Europe committed billions of euros to support refugees and the communities hosting them. The EU’s Facility for Refugees in Turkey eventually reached six billion euros. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan repeatedly threatened to “open the gates” and send millions of refugees toward Europe if Ankara did not receive greater political and financial support. In February 2020, the threat became policy. Turkey announced it would no longer stop migrants trying to reach the Greek and Bulgarian borders, and thousands headed toward the crossings. The move came amid fighting in Syria and Turkish demands for stronger European backing. Europe discovered that the agreement that had dramatically reduced arrivals on the Greek islands had also created deep dependence on Ankara. Disputes over money, visas, Syria or relations with Erdoğan could suddenly become direct threats to Europe’s external border. At Europe’s eastern frontier, the use of migrants became even more confrontational. In 2021, the EU, Poland, Lithuania and Latvia accused Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s government of helping bring migrants, particularly from the Middle East, to Minsk and then moving them toward the EU border. The EU Agency for Asylum concluded that Belarus had taken measures designed to facilitate irregular migration first toward Lithuania and later toward Latvia and Poland. Brussels described the move as a “hybrid attack” intended to retaliate against European sanctions and destabilize member states. Belarus and Russia denied organizing the flow. In that case, Europe was not paying a neighboring state to guard its border. Instead, it was confronting a hostile government accused of exploiting the same vulnerability against it. Migrants trying to reach Europe became trapped between Belarusian forces pushing them westward and Polish forces preventing them from entering, often in freezing conditions and without adequate protection. The lesson was similar: Migration is not only a humanitarian or economic issue. When large numbers of people move over a short period, migration can become an instrument of foreign policy, placing pressure on governments, deepening divisions inside the EU and strengthening anti-immigration parties. Europe’s policy of externalizing its borders carries another cost. The more responsibility for stopping migration is transferred to countries outside European territory, the further migrants, refugees and asylum seekers are pushed away from Europe’s courts, regulators and media scrutiny. Libya offers the starkest example. For years, the EU and individual member states have provided equipment, training and funding to the Libyan coast guard to intercept boats and return passengers to Libya. Human rights organizations say many of those returned are sent to detention centers where torture, sexual violence, extortion, forced labor and arbitrary detention have been documented. Brussels says its assistance includes oversight mechanisms, efforts against trafficking networks and voluntary return programs that help migrants go back to their countries of origin. Critics, however, argue that Europe is effectively paying others to carry out actions it could not conduct in the same way on its own territory, while distancing itself from legal and public responsibility for the consequences. Similar criticism has been directed at cooperation with Tunisia, Morocco and Egypt. Governments with controversial human rights records receive money, equipment and political legitimacy because Europe considers them essential to securing its borders. As fear of migration grows within EU member states, critics argue, Europe’s willingness to impose conditions or challenge its partners diminishes. Who holds the key? Europe’s strategy is not without achievements. Cooperation with transit countries can save lives, dismantle smuggling networks, create legal routes for migration and prevent people from embarking on dangerous journeys. Countries such as Morocco, Tunisia and Mauritania are not merely European gatekeepers. They also face migration pressure of their own, have long borders to police and host substantial migrant and refugee populations. But the more the European Union relies on non-member states, the more control it effectively transfers to them. European money can buy cooperation, but it cannot guarantee it indefinitely. An economic crisis, a diplomatic confrontation, a demand for political recognition or simply an enforcement failure can reopen a route that Europe believed had been closed. The current breach in Ceuta does not prove that Morocco deliberately activated migration pressure in the same way Spain accused it of doing in 2021. Spanish intelligence does not appear to believe Rabat created the latest migration wave from nothing. Social media rumors, the court ruling and economic distress helped drive thousands of people toward the border. But when they arrived, the country Europe pays to stop them allowed them to cross, according to the assessment. The episode shows that Europe’s border does not end at Ceuta’s fences, Greece’s coastline or the waters off Italy. It begins at Libyan coast guard bases, Moroccan police checkpoints, Tunisian and Mauritanian ports and negotiating tables in Ankara. The valve controlling the flow of migrants into Europe is often located outside Europe itself, in the hands of governments that understand exactly how much that leverage is worth.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: The man, who did not wish to be named, has lived in Sweden since 2017 with his wife, who is Swedish. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The man, who did not wish to be named, has lived in Sweden since 2017 with his wife, who is Swedish. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Sweden Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene Case is latest in string of post-Brexit deportations from country, which has been criticised for high refusal rate for British people to remain Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Thu 3 Sep 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 3 Sep 2026 05.07 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The wife of a British man detained by police in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation has pleaded with Andy Burnham to get involved in the Brexit catastrophe unfolding for many British citizens in Sweden. Charles, who does not want to be fully identified, and his Swedish wife, Lily, were summoned to the police station at 10am on Tuesday, where he was told he would be held at a detention centre and deported within the next two weeks. Lily, who is a lawyer, was told to go home and get his passport despite her protests that there was a court process under way appealing the deportation order. “I feel shame,” said Lily, who asked that their family’s surname not be published. “To me, Britain represents freedom for human beings, and then to see this British man in detention just because he wants to be with his wife and live in his house, this is not right. “What kind of country are we living in? Is this civilisation? They don’t care about human rights. This is a European country, but it looks like Sweden is like somewhere like Afghanistan,” she said. Lily met her husband in the UK after starting a law degree in London in 2010. She now works for the local authority in Stockholm and returned to Sweden in 2015, with her soon-to-be husband joining her in 2017, three years before Brexit. A former business consultant, now retired, Charles made an application to remain in the country before the deadline for applications after Brexit. His application was rejected two years later in 2022 and the family have been fighting deportation ever since with “six or seven” appeals, said Lily. “The Migration Agency has hunted us for five years.” During the summer the couple received a text asking them to show up at their local police station on 1 September. “They told us they needed to talk and we should show up at 10am. They didn’t say anything about deportation or to bring passports. “When we arrived they told us that they needed to talk to Charles privately, and after three hours they told me they were taking him to the detention centre and that they would deport him. “I told them that they can’t do this because his case is in court and they have to wait for the outcome, but they told me they were going ahead,” said Lily. She has pleaded with Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, to intervene. “Why can’t Andy Burnham talk to the Swedish government? How many British families have to suffer in Sweden before Andy Burnham gets involved? How many families have to leave their homes, be forced into selling their houses? “This is not humanity. This is not right. They should threaten the trade agreement,” she added. Charles’s case comes amid growing controversy over Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement, which is supposed to have protected EU citizens in the UK and British citizens settled in the bloc before Brexit. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Among those threatened with removal in the past month are 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, who has been in the country for 21 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old man in dementia care who has been in the country for 24 years. A 34-year-old man revealed this week he was deported from Sweden in January despite having been in the country since he was 10 and being married to a Swedish woman in Gothenburg. Two years ago another British woman, Kathleen Poole, was threatened with deportation because she had not provided financial statements to the Migration Agency while in full-time dementia care. The Swedish migration minister defended the country’s implementation of the withdrawal agreement, saying the Migration Agency was following the rules and had granted a number of residency permits for Britons who had “reasonable grounds” for late applications. However, concerns have been raised formally by the UK government through the EU-UK specialised committee, the official platform to raise issues over the working out of the Brexit deal, over the high number of late applications for post Brexit residency being rejected. Sweden, along with 12 other EU member states, opted for a constitutive system requiring citizens to formally apply to extend their residency rights post Brexit. Others, like Spain, opted for a declaratory system requiring Britons to simply register their presence initially. Lily says she and her husband phoned the authorities and used the correct form for residency and have been fighting ever since. The latest statistics from the 2024 European Commission annual report show that 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency have been decided in Sweden. According to analysis by the UK government, 27.5% (3,918) of applications have been refused, “a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3 and 4%”. Sources added that this “constitutes 12% of all refusals across the EU member states, even though UK nationals in Sweden makes up only 1.55% of the total population of WA beneficiaries in EU member states”. Denmark faced a similar controversy two years ago, but legislation was introduced to give British nationals a second chance to make the residency application. https://www.politico.eu/article/exit-pol.text: BERLIN — Germany’s far right is on track to claim its biggest electoral success since World War II, with projections showing it will win more than 44 percent of the vote in the eastern region of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday. The election is seen a key test of whether the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — now comfortably the most popular party in the EU’s biggest economy — is capable of governing. According to a projection by the broadcaster ARD, the AfD was on course to secure a landslide first place, with 44.4 percent of the vote. Advertisement Advertisement The same projection put the Christian Democratic Union party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz in second place, on 18.5 percent — a devastating collapse from the 37. 1 percent it scored in 2021. The success of the anti-immigrant AfD in this small state of just 2.1 million inhabitants is a huge blow to his conservatives, and has even sparked speculation about a potential Kanzlertausch , or chancellor swap. The big question on Sunday night is whether the AfD’s lead will ultimately be large enough for it to govern, or whether other parties will be able to form a coalition against it. The AfD’s national co-leader Alice Weidel immediately hailed a “historic result” and said the party had “a very clear mandate for governing.” But the election night arithmetic is still uncertain. If the final results are in line with the projections, the AfD will fall very narrowly short of being able to govern outright in the state parliament. Much attention will therefore fall on the populist Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance party (BSW), which appears close to the 5 percent threshold of qualifying for Saxony-Anhalt’s regional parliament. The BSW has said it would be willing to cooperate with the AfD, and could secure the election for the far right. Advertisement Advertisement Weidel said her party “always has an outstretched hand” for coalition partners. Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt, was wary on the question of whether he would be able to become prime minster of the region. “We can’t answer that question right now at 6 p.m. But we’ve achieved exactly what we set out to do. We’ve made history in this state,” he told ARD. He argued the result was a direct signal to Merz. “Of course, it’s also a message directed at Berlin. We’re well aware that he’s a very effective campaigner. For us, Friedrich Merz was the face of this campaign. Each day of having this man in the chancellery is one too many. That’s how people in Saxony-Anhalt see it, too.” Body blow to Merz The result looks set to be a bruising blow for the CDU that has governed the region over the past 24 years. CDU General Secretary Franziska Hoppermann called it a”very difficult result” and an “overall defeat” for the Christian Democrats. Sven Schulze, the current prime minister of Saxony-Anhalt, also conceded the severity of the defeat, particularly since turnout appeared to be very high. Advertisement Advertisement “The winner of the election, the AfD, is now the strongest force in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt, and we in the CDU will have to deal with this result,” he said. The fact that four in 10 voters in Saxony-Anhalt supported the AfD despite its state branch being designated a right-wing extremist organization by the state’s intelligence agency and reports that members of lead candidate Siegmund’s inner circle were part of an organization modeled on the Hitler Youth , speaks to widespread public distrust in mainstream parties, the media, and institutions in eastern Germany — a region that was under communist control during the Cold War. The party achieved its best result since its founding in 2013 by vowing to deport migrants with a “remigration offensive,” to push for closer relations with Moscow — including by bringing back school exchange programs with Russia — to remove rainbow flags from schools, introduce a “baby welcome grant” of €2,000 for the first two children and €4,000 for each additional child. The party also pledged to reform school curricula to lesson material on Germany’s Nazi past in an effort to end what some of its politicians call a “guilt cult.” However, the party’s success was apparently due less to its own pledges than to voters’ rejection of mainstream parties, particularly Merz and his conservative bloc. Only 9 percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt approved of Merz’s performance, according to an ARD exit poll. Saxony-Anhalt is the German state with the lowest average net income, and economic anxiety — over declining industry and rising energy costs — was a major factor motivating voters. Seventy percent said they were “greatly worried” that rising prices would prevent them from paying their bills, according to an ARD survey, while 58 percent feared they would be unable to maintain their standard of living. Polls show that the AfD is also leading in the eastern state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania, where voters go to the ballot on Sept. 20. In Berlin, a traditionally left-wing capital where voters will go to the polls that same day, the AfD is also performing particularly strongly, polling at around 18 percent. The Saxony-Anhalt result surpasses the AfD’s previous biggest breakthrough in the eastern region of Thuringia, where it won 32.8 percent of the vote in 2024. After that election, the CDU needed to form a minority coalition with left-wing parties. This story is being updated. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.cnb.cz/en/cnb-news/press-rel.text: Home News archive Press releases Press releases 1. 10. 2026 Others Treasury offers municipalities and regions an attractive savings account with immediate access to funds Share Municipalities and regions will be able to use a new savings account in the Treasury from 1 October. Developed by the Czech National Bank (CNB) in cooperation with the Ministry of Finance, the new product combines the benefits of a current account and a savings account. It will offer local authorities attractive remuneration of 3.7% without requiring them to give up immediate access to their deposited funds. They will be able to manage their deposited funds through the CNB’s modern and user-friendly ABO-K internet banking application. The new product expands the range of modern financial services offered by the Treasury, which the CNB operates for the Ministry of Finance. As a result, the remuneration offered is competitive with accounts available from commercial banks. “The Treasury is becoming ever faster and simpler. Last year, we introduced instant payments, so funds are now credited to state accounts immediately. Today, we are adding a savings account that municipalities and regions can open electronically and manage from anywhere. No paperwork, no waiting at the counter. As the bank of the state, we want to provide services of a high standard,” said CNB Governor Aleš Michl. “Liquidity 2.0 is a solution that benefits municipalities, regions, the state and, above all, citizens, who rightly expect public funds to be managed efficiently. Local authorities will have an opportunity to earn attractive remuneration in a completely safe manner. Thanks to more efficient management of voluntarily deposited funds, the state will reduce its dependence on, and need for, more expensive financing on the financial market and lower debt servicing costs. At the same time, municipalities and regions will not lose control of a single koruna,” said Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance Alena Schillerová. “As before, we will continue with prudent but active cash pooling. Only a stable portion of the newly deposited funds may in future reduce the need to issue additional government bonds, while the necessary reserve will remain safely and short-term remunerated so that local authorities continue to enjoy full access to their funds, just as they do at their banks. The new product may therefore gradually reduce interest costs, ease pressure on growth in government debt and ultimately improve the state’s financial position,” added Petr Pavelek, Director of the Debt and Financial Assets Management Department at the Ministry of Finance. From 1 October 2026, a savings account may be opened in the same way as a current account, i.e. entirely electronically, without the need to visit a CNB branch. Municipalities and regions will manage the account via ABO‑K, a modern and user-friendly internet banking application that offers straightforward operation and an immediate overview of all funds. The new service is therefore available to all municipalities and regions in the Czech Republic regardless of their location or distance from a CNB branch. The new CNB savings account may be used to receive and send day-to-day payments, and debit cards may also be used with the account. At the same time, it offers remuneration of funds in the form of a monetary payment in lieu of interest, currently set at 3.7% p.a. Local authorities can thus manage their available funds and earn remuneration on them efficiently and transparently in one place, without the need to transfer them between a current account and a savings account. The new account may be opened with the CNB by territorial self-governing units, i.e. municipalities and regions, as well as voluntary associations of municipalities and communities of municipalities. Account holders will receive remuneration in the form of a monetary payment in lieu of interest, which is paid by the Ministry of Finance. The rate is determined by the Ministry of Finance and published on its website (in Czech only). https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, previously warned any restriction to Starshield system would ‘bring a lot of human losses’. Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPA View image in fullscreen Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, previously warned any restriction to Starshield system would ‘bring a lot of human losses’. Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPA Ukraine Ukraine’s military says Starlink satellite connection stable after recent restrictions Volodymyr Zelenskyy offers thanks to US allies for restoring system key to air defence and ‘frontline logistics’ Donna Ferguson Sat 24 Oct 2026 11.47 EDT First published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 11.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government has said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted . The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month. The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US. The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel , although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine. “I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive. However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.” Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration , writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote. View image in fullscreen Musk blamed the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X that the systems were ‘owned and controlled by the US government’. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.” There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.” He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming whom in the Ukraine-Starlink row? Read more Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for ‌today is that Starlink ‌and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the ‌level we need.” The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.” On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning. When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.” He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person. https://www.novinky.cz/clanek/zahranicni.text: Chcete-li článek poslouchat, přihlaste se Při zřícení vojenského vrtulníku Black Hawk u města Malatya na jihovýchodě Turecka zahynuli čtyři vojáci. O incidentu ve čtvrtek večer informovala turecká média. Americký vrtulník UH-60 Blackhawk. Ilustrační snímek Turecký vojenský vrtulník S-70 Black Hawk se zřítil ve čtvrti Yeşilyurt. „Jeden z našich vrtulníků typu S-70 havaroval v Malatyi z dosud neznámých příčin. K místu havárie se již dostali záchranáři a okamžitě zahájili pátrací a záchranné práce,“ citoval server Cumhurriyet turecké ministerstvo obrany. Při nehodě, jejíž příčina zatím není podle ministerstva jasná, zahynuli čtyři vojáci. Po pádu vrtulník začal hořet a vítr plameny rozšířil na blízké budovy. https://hvg.hu/itthon/20261113_a-nato-ka.text: Oroszország hosszú távú fenyegetést jelent az euroatlanti biztonságra – mondta Giuseppe Cavo Dragone admirális, akit Sándor Zsolt vezérkari főnök fogadott. A Magyar Honvédség felkészült az esetleges külföldi szabotázsakciók kivédésére, amelyet a szükséges nemzetbiztonsági eszközökkel és a megfelelő létszámú katonai személyzettel biztosít – jelentette ki Sándor Zsolt vezérezredes, a Honvéd Vezérkar főnöke, miután a Stefánia-palotában fogadta a Budapestre érkező Giuseppe Cavo Dragone admirálist, a NATO Katonai Bizottságának elnökét. „Szilárdan hiszem, hogy szövetségünk ereje nem csupán katonai képességeinkben rejlik, hanem a szövetségesek között kiépített bizalomban, szolidaritásban és személyes kapcsolatokban is” – fogalmazott a vezérkari főnök. Hozzátette, hogy Magyarország kiveszi részét a feladatokból, köztük a szövetség keleti határának védelméből és a Nyugat-Balkán stabilitásának elősegítéséből, a koszovói és bosznia-hercegovinai nemzetközi békefenntartó missziókban való szerepvállalásával. Cavo Dragone elmondta: „Biztonsági környezetünk továbbra is az elmúlt évtizedek legnehezebbike, Oroszország hosszú távú fenyegetést jelent az euroatlanti biztonságra nézve”, és hozzátette, hogy Moszkva agresszív magatartása nem korlátozódik Ukrajnára. Kijelentette, hogy az egész szövetség hibrid támadásokkal szembesül, amelyek eszköztárába a kibertámadás, a légtérsértés, a GPS-jelzavarás és a dezinformáció tartozik. Washington rég nem látott hitelességgel töltötte meg a NATO elrettentésének és védelmének új koncepcióját. A hagyományos konfliktusokra megalkotott teória működőképessé tételéhez sok munka vezet, miközben a háborús küszöb alatti hibrid támadások elszaporodtak. „Egyetlen szövetségesünk sem mentes ezektől a hibrid fenyegetésektől, és mi ezeket nagyon komolyan vesszük. A NATO erre úgy reagál, hogy megosztja a hírszerzési információkat, védi a kritikus infrastruktúrát, és megerősíti jelenlétét ott, ahol arra szükség van” – fogalmazott. Felhívta a figyelmet a nemzeti ellenállóképességre, amit erős intézmények, a védett hálózatok és tájékozott polgárok szavatolnak. Mind a két fél kiemelte a NATO Közép-európai Többnemzeti Hadosztály jelentőségét, amelynek most először tölti be magyar katona a parancsnoki tisztségét Antal László vezérőrnagy személyében. A NATO politikai döntéshozatali és katonai szervezetei közötti intézményi kapcsolat fenntartásáért felelős admirális elmondta: a Magyarországon tett két és fél napos látogatásán a Bakonyban megtekintette a NATO Előretolt Szárazföldi Többnemzeti Harccsoport bemutatóját, tárgyalt a magyar honvédelmi és külügyminiszterrel , és találkozott az Országgyűlés két bizottságának elnökével . A találkozó azonban egyelőre nem jött össze, mivel a neki szánt csomagot otthon hagyták, ezért vissza kellett menniük Székesfehérvárra. Első látásra semmi gyanús nem volt a hagyományos indiai édességben.
